Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The first five paragraphs effectively use summary and exposition to compress roughly fourteen years of history—establishing the narrator's relationship with Q, Q's effortless charm during their college years, and the ten-year gap after graduation. This background information is essential for building the mythos of Q as a "golden boy" who never experiences social friction. 

The remainder of the story transitions into a vivid, real-time scene at the Rockaway Bathing Club. By dramatizing the tense conversation between Q and Meredith through sharp dialogue and specific physical actions, the story allows the reader to witness the unraveling of Q's charm firsthand. The initial summary provides the necessary context to make the climax of the scene—where Q's effortless facade finally cracks in the face of corporate reality—meaningful and impactful.
